name: Week in Review
desc: Finish sentences about your week and add details.
instr: Choose three sentences and finish them about your week. Add a detail or an example to each one.
cards: A small win this week was…
I wish I'd had more time to…
The best moment of my week was…
Next week I'm looking forward to…
coverP: a weekly planner open on a desk with a coffee, a pen and sticky notes

name: Strange Delivery
desc: A mystery parcel arrives. What do you do with it?
instr: A parcel arrives at your door with no note. Choose one item. What would you do or say, and why?
ph: The first thing I'd do is…
cards: A plane ticket to a secret destination
A cake with your face on it
A letter from your future self
A suitcase full of old coins
imgP: an open cardboard parcel on a doorstep containing {x}

name: My Go-To
desc: Your favourite, always-reliable choices.
instr: Your 'go-to' is the thing you always choose. Pick three and explain them in 2–3 sentences each.
coverP: a cosy flat lay of favourite everyday things: a mug, headphones, a snack, a book and trainers

name: Main Character
desc: Today your life is a film. Describe it.
instr: Imagine today is a film and you are the main character. Answer the questions with true details.
ph: In the background you can hear…
cards: What's the title of the film?
coverP: an old cinema clapperboard and a film camera on a city street at golden hour

name: Mood Menu
desc: Order one to three 'moods' that match how you feel.
instr: This is today's mood menu. Order one to three options that match how you feel right now and say why.
ph: Right now I'm in the mood for…
cards: Stay under a blanket all day
imgP: a cosy scene that captures the mood: {x}

name: Ideal Weekend
desc: Plan your perfect weekend in detail.
instr: Imagine your perfect weekend. Answer the questions with as many details as you can.
cards: What time would you wake up?
Who would you spend it with?
What would you do on Sunday night?
coverP: a sunny Saturday morning: breakfast on a balcony with a view

name: How Often?
desc: Say how often you do everyday things and why.
instr: Read the card. How often do you do this? Say why.
imgP: an everyday scene illustrating the activity '{x}'

name: Name Three
desc: Name three things for each card, then compare.
instr: Read the card and name three things. Then compare with your classmates. Did anyone say the same?
cards: things you take to the beach
things you do before school or work
things you can buy with 5 euros
animals you can see on a farm
things you have in your pocket
imgP: a scene representing the category '{x}', showing several examples

name: I Use It For…
desc: Look at the object and say how you use it.
instr: Look at the picture. Think about your life. Say two or three sentences about how you use it.

name: Define It
desc: Write your own definition with three ideas.
instr: Create your own definition. Use three simple ideas or examples.
ex: A lazy Sunday: It's a day when you don't set an alarm. Usually, it means staying in your pyjamas. For me, it's when I watch films all afternoon.
coverP: an open dictionary on a wooden table with a magnifying glass

name: My User Manual
desc: Finish sentences from your own 'instruction manual'.
instr: Imagine you come with an instruction manual. Finish the sentence with something true about you and give an example.
cards: If you want to make me happy, …
If I go quiet, it means…
The best way to cheer me up is…
If you invite me to dinner, …
If you send me a message, …
coverP: an open instruction manual booklet next to a cup of tea

name: Five-Star Review
desc: Rate a life experience from 1 to 5 stars, like an online review.
instr: Rate this experience from 1 to 5 stars. Tell the story behind your rating: what happened, the best part, the worst part, and would you recommend it?
cards: Your first day at a new school or job
imgP: a scene representing the experience: {x}

name: Red Flag, Green Flag
desc: Share your own red and green flags in a situation.
instr: Read the situation. What's your own red flag and green flag here? Then talk about common ones people have.
ph: A green flag for me is when someone…
I have to admit I tend to…
coverP: a red flag and a green flag waving on a beach against a blue sky

name: The Great Swap
desc: Keep the first option or swap it for the second?
instr: Would you keep the first option or swap it for the second one? Give at least one reason.

cards.b: A walk in a snowy forest
Rainy nights with a blanket and a film

name: Done, Try or Skip
desc: Three activities: which have you done, which would you try, which would you skip?
instr: Look at the three activities. Which one have you done? Which would you love to try? Which would you skip?
cards: Spend a day without your phone
Visit a country where you don't speak the language
Dye your hair a crazy colour
Try a food you can't pronounce
imgP: the activity: {x}

name: Two Truths and a Lie
desc: Say three things about yourself. The others find the lie.
instr: Use the topic on the card. Say three sentences about yourself: two are true, one is a lie. The others ask up to three questions, then vote.
ph: I think number … is the lie because…
ex: Topic: food. 1) I once ate a cricket. 2) I can't stand chocolate. 3) My grandmother taught me to make paella.
end: Who was the best liar? Which lie was the hardest to spot?
coverP: a detective magnifying glass over three paper cards on a table

name: Unwritten Rules
desc: Is it OK or not OK? Talk about the rules nobody writes down.
instr: Read the situation. Is it OK or not? Is there an unwritten rule about it? Give your opinion and an example.
cards: Reclining your seat on a short flight
Leaving a group chat without saying anything
Arriving 15 minutes late to a party
Going to a dinner without bringing anything
Taking a phone call in a restaurant
Asking someone how much they earn
Sending a voice message longer than two minutes
Sitting next to a stranger on an empty bus
Watching the next episode of a series without your partner
Eating someone else's food in the office fridge
Not replying to a message for three days
imgP: an everyday scene of this situation: {x}

name: There's a Catch
desc: A dream offer… with conditions in the small print.
instr: This offer sounds like a dream! Add 3–5 conditions that make it less attractive. Would your partner still say yes?
ph: Oh, and you'll also have to…
ex: A free house by the sea… but you can never leave the town, you must paint it pink every year, and the neighbours are 30 seagulls.
cards: A free house by the sea
Unlimited free flights for a year
Your favourite singer plays at your birthday
A month off with full pay
Speaking every language in the world
A holiday on a private island
imgP: a dreamy, attractive photo of: {x}

name: The Job Nobody Wants
desc: Would you accept these small, annoying roles?
instr: Read the role. Would you accept it?
q: Would you accept this role? Why or why not?
What would be difficult about it?
ph: I'd be happy to… as long as…
cards: The friend who drives everyone home after the party
The one who tells the group the trip is cancelled
The person who collects the money for a present
The one who always carries the heaviest bag
The one who tests the water before everyone swims
The person who reads all the terms and conditions
The one who wakes everyone up on holiday
The neighbour who keeps everyone's spare keys
The one who chooses the music in the car
The person who writes the group's birthday messages
The one who orders for the whole table
The person who has to say no to the boss
imgP: a slightly funny everyday scene of: {x}

name: Designed to Hook You
desc: How do products keep us coming back?
instr: How was this designed to keep people using it? What makes it attractive, fun or hard to stop?
ph: What makes it so effective is…
ex: Streaks in a language app: missing a day feels like losing something you've built, so you open the app even when you're tired.
cards: New clothes in shops every week
imgP: a photo representing: {x} (generic, no real brands or app logos)

name: Convenient or Creepy?
desc: Technology that helps… and watches.
instr: Is this convenient, creepy or both? What are the benefits and the privacy risks? Where would you draw the line?
ph: I can see the benefits, especially if…
I'd accept it as long as…
That's where I'd draw the line.
cards: Your fridge orders milk when it runs out
A shop recognises your face and greets you by name
Your car tells your insurance company how you drive
Your phone suggests replies that sound exactly like you
Your smartwatch alerts your doctor automatically
An app knows when you're about to cancel
A school uses cameras to check students' attention
Your smart speaker is always listening for its name
Your bank predicts you'll run out of money
Your boss can see how much you type
Your family can always see your location
Ads for something you only talked about
imgP: a photo of this technology scenario: {x}

name: Parallel Realities
desc: Find the deeper connection between two very different ideas.
instr: Look beyond the surface. What do these two ideas have in common at a deeper level?
ph: At their core, both are about…
In both cases, you have to…

name: Headline vs Real Life
desc: Does an imagined headline match your experience?
instr: Imagine you read this headline. Does it match what you see in real life?
q: Does it sound believable? Why or why not?
Does your own experience support it or challenge it?
Why might real life be different from the data?
ph: People tend to say one thing and do another.

cards.s: 7 in 10 people check their phone within 10 minutes of waking up
cards.q: Is that a problem, or just modern life?

cards.s: Most people say they would earn less to work four days a week
cards.q: Would you? What would you do with the extra day?

cards.s: 6 in 10 students say exams don't show what they really know
cards.q: What would be a fairer way to assess students?

cards.s: Most drivers think they're better than average
cards.q: Why are we so bad at judging ourselves?

cards.s: 1 in 3 adults has never cooked a full meal from scratch
cards.q: Is cooking still an essential skill?

cards.s: Most people prefer texting to phone calls
cards.q: When is a call still better?

cards.s: Half of people have bought something online they never used
cards.q: What makes us buy things we don't need?

cards.s: 4 in 10 people say they work better from home
cards.q: What do we lose when we don't share an office?

cards.s: Most people say they'd quit social media for a year if you paid them
cards.q: How much would someone have to pay you?

cards.s: Most people say they want to travel more sustainably, but flights keep growing
cards.q: Whose responsibility is it: people's or governments'?

note: These headlines are invented for discussion, not real statistics.
coverP: a pile of newspapers and a smartphone showing a chart, on a café table

name: Defend the Object
desc: Convince everyone that an ordinary object is the best invention ever.
instr: Convince everyone that this is the most important invention of all time. How has it changed people's lives?
end: Vote: which object won the debate?

name: Would You Rather
desc: Pick a side and give two reasons.
instr: Choose one option and give two reasons. Then try to defend the other one!
imgP: a photo representing: {x}

name: Speed Debate
desc: Two minutes per side on light, funny motions.
instr: Side A argues for, side B argues against. Two minutes each, then 30 seconds to reply.
cards: Breakfast is the most important meal
Everyone should learn to cook at school
It's OK to recline your seat on a plane
Board games are better than video games
end: Class vote: which debate was the most convincing?
imgP: a playful photo representing the topic: {x}

name: Just a Minute
desc: Talk for 60 seconds without hesitating or repeating.
instr: Speak for one minute about the topic. No long pauses, no repeating yourself, don't go off topic!
cards: The best smell in the world

name: Fortunately, Unfortunately
desc: Build a silly story with alternating good and bad news.
instr: Continue the story. Take turns: one sentence starts with 'Fortunately…', the next with 'Unfortunately…'.
cards: I woke up late on Monday.
I found a wallet in the street.
My best friend invited me to a party.
The plane landed in the wrong country.
My phone fell into the sea.
The teacher gave us a surprise test.
imgP: the story moment: {x}

name: Alibi
desc: Two suspects, one story. Find the differences.
instr: Two suspects plan their alibi for the time of the 'crime' outside the room (5 minutes). The detectives prepare questions. Then each suspect is questioned alone.
q: Where were you between 7 and 9 pm?
ph: Are you sure? Your partner said…
cards: Someone ate the teacher's birthday cake.
Someone painted a moustache on the head teacher's portrait.
All the classroom chairs are on the roof.
The neighbour's garden gnome has gone missing.
Someone changed every phone alarm to 4 am.
The last slice of pizza vanished from the staff room.
Someone hid the TV remote, and the final is tonight.
end: Guilty or not guilty? If their stories differ in three details, they're guilty!
imgP: a funny scene of the aftermath: {x}

name: Taboo
desc: Describe the word without the forbidden words.
instr: Projected version: one student sits with their back to the screen. Their team describes the word without saying the forbidden words. Printed version: students take a card and describe it to their team.
coverP: a stack of blank game cards and a sand timer on a table

name: Desert Island
desc: Agree on the five things to take with you.
instr: Your group is going to live on a desert island for a month. You can only take five things. Agree together in 8 minutes.
ph: I think we should take… because…
end: Each group presents its five items. Which group would survive?
imgP: {x} lying on a sandy tropical beach

name: Hot Seat
desc: Interview a student who plays a role.
instr: One student sits in the hot seat and plays the role on the card. The class asks questions for three minutes.
q: What's a normal day like for you?
What's the best and worst part?
cards: A teacher on the last day of school
A chef at a busy restaurant
A ghost in an old castle
printNote: Guessing version: give the student a secret role card. The class asks yes/no questions until someone guesses who they are.
imgP: {x}, shown through their setting, uniform or tools

name: Story Chain
desc: Tell a story together using three random words.
instr: Tell a story together. Each person adds one or two sentences and must use one of the words, with a linker.

name: Fake Definitions
desc: A real but very strange English word. Invent a convincing definition and fool the others.
instr: This is a real English word. Invent a definition that sounds true. Then everyone votes for the one they believe. The next slide shows the real meaning.
ph: For example: 'My uncle is a real…'
I'm sure it means… because it sounds like…

cards.ans: a fuss or commotion, usually about something unimportant
in the opposite direction to the sun; anticlockwise
a nervous feeling in your stomach
to waste time doing nothing useful
the pleasant smell of rain on dry ground
a silly person who talks too much
to leave or run away very quickly
crooked, not in a straight line
small bits and pieces, or gadgets you don't know the name of
a clever but dishonest person, especially a politician
to leave suddenly without saying goodbye

ind: Show the word. You and the student each invent a definition and say an example sentence.
Mix in the real definition (don't show the next slide yet) and let the student guess which is real.
Reveal and compare. Swap roles: the student reads three definitions to you.
pair: Show the word. Each pair writes one fake definition and one example sentence.
Pairs read their definition to another pair, who guess if it's real.
Reveal the real meaning on the next slide.
grp: Show the word. Teams of 3 write a convincing fake definition in 2 minutes.
Collect them, add the real one (read it from the next slide without showing it) and read all aloud.
Everyone votes. A team scores 1 point for each vote its fake gets, and 2 points for guessing the real one. Then reveal.

end: Which fake definition was the most convincing today?

name: Sell It To Me
desc: Combine two random things into a product and pitch it to a very specific customer.
instr: Combine the two things into one product, then sell it to this customer. You have one minute to convince them!
ph: It's perfect for someone like you because…

cards.t: Customer: a grandmother who loves gardening
Customer: a teenager who never wakes up on time

ind: Show the card. Give the student one minute to prepare and one minute to pitch.
You play the customer: ask difficult questions and raise objections.
Swap roles on the next card.
pair: One student is the seller, the other is the customer, who must play the role on the card.
Seller pitches for one minute, then the customer asks two questions and decides: buy or not?
Swap roles.
grp: In teams, students get two minutes to invent the product and its name.
One person per team pitches to the class, who play the customer.
Class votes for the product they'd actually buy.

end: Which product would actually sell? What would you call it?

name: Excuses, Excuses
desc: Invent the most creative excuse for an awkward situation.
instr: You're in trouble! Invent the most creative (but believable) excuse. Then the others decide if they believe you.
cards: You arrive 40 minutes late to your best friend's birthday dinner.
You forgot to do your homework, again.
You ate your flatmate's birthday cake.
Your teacher sees you on social media when you said you were ill.
You lost the keys to a friend's car.
You fell asleep in an important meeting.
Your dog is in the swimming pool of the hotel.
You broke your neighbour's window with a ball.
You sent a message about your boss… to your boss.
You missed your own surprise party.
You're wearing two different shoes at an interview.

ind: Show the situation. The student gives an excuse; you react as the angry person and ask questions.
Push for details until the story falls apart (or doesn't!).
Swap: you give an excuse and the student judges it.
pair: Student A is in trouble, Student B is the angry person. A has 30 seconds to explain.
B asks three follow-up questions, then decides: forgive or not?
Swap roles on the next card.
grp: Show the situation and give everyone 30 seconds to think.
Pick three students to give their excuse.
The class votes: most creative and most believable.

end: Who gave the best excuse today?

name: Hot Takes
desc: Controversial (but harmless) opinions. Agree, disagree and defend your position.
instr: Here's a hot take. Do you agree or disagree? Take a side and defend it, even if it's a silly one.
cards: Cereal is a type of soup.
Phone calls are worse than going to the dentist.
Breakfast food is better at dinner time.
Sequels are usually better than the original film.
Sandwiches taste better when they're cut into triangles.
It's rude to send a voice message.
Weekends should be three days long.
Socks with sandals are a good idea.
Going to the gym is boring.

ind: Show the hot take. The student says agree or disagree on a 1–10 scale and why.
You take the opposite side, even if you agree, and argue back.
Ask them to find one argument for the other side.
pair: Partners each give a number from 1 (totally disagree) to 10 (totally agree).
The person with the lower number must convince the other to move at least two points.
Swap who starts on the next card.
grp: Show the hot take. Students stand on an imaginary line: one wall = agree, other wall = disagree.
Ask students at both ends to defend their position.
Anyone can move if they're convinced. Ask the people who moved why.

end: Which hot take divided the class the most?

name: Most Likely To…
desc: Who in the class is most likely to…? Nominate someone and explain why.
instr: Who in this class is most likely to do this? Choose a classmate (or yourself!) and explain why. Keep it kind!
ph: I think … is most likely to… because…
I'd say me, to be honest, because…
cards: get lost in their own city
arrive late to their own wedding

ind: Private student version: ask 'Who in your family / group of friends is most likely to…?' and let them explain.
Ask for a real story that proves it.
Answer one yourself.
pair: Pairs think of people they both know (classmates, famous people).
They agree on one name per card and give a reason.
Compare with another pair.
grp: Show the card. On 3, everyone points at a classmate.
The student with most fingers pointing at them asks two people why.
Keep it light: ban answers that could be hurtful.

end: Who got the most votes today? Do they agree?

name: Silly Conspiracies
desc: Convince the class of a completely absurd (and harmless) conspiracy theory.
instr: Your job is to convince everyone this is true. Invent 'evidence', use statistics and sound very serious.
ph: Think about it: why else would…?
cards: Cats invented the internet so we'd post photos of them.
The moon is made of cheese, and astronauts keep it secret.
Socks disappear because washing machines eat them.
Every time you sneeze, a cloud is born.
Dogs can read, but they pretend they can't.
Mondays were invented by coffee companies.
Your fridge light stays on when the door is closed.
Penguins can fly, but only when nobody is looking.

ind: Give the student two minutes to prepare three pieces of 'evidence'.
You play the sceptic and ask tricky questions.
Then swap: you defend one and they attack.
pair: Student A defends the theory for one minute; Student B is the sceptical journalist.
B must ask at least three questions starting 'But how do you explain…?'
Swap roles on the next card.
grp: Groups of three prepare the 'evidence' in three minutes.
One speaker per group presents. The class asks questions.
Vote: which group was the most convincing?

end: Which theory was so convincing you almost believed it?

name: The Pitch
desc: Dragons' Den style: pitch a ridiculous invention and get investors to say yes.
instr: You're on a TV show for inventors. Pitch this invention in one minute. The investors will ask questions and decide if they invest.
ph: Our product solves a problem everyone has:…
We're asking for… in exchange for…
cards: A fridge that locks itself at midnight
Shoes that tell you when you're lost
A pillow that records your dreams
A mug that keeps coffee hot for a week
An app that replies to messages for you
A sofa that makes you do exercise
A pen that corrects your spelling

ind: The student pitches; you're the investor and ask the three questions.
Decide: invest or not? Explain why.
Swap: you pitch the next one.
pair: Each pair pitches to another pair, who play investors.
Investors must ask at least three questions, then decide.
Swap roles.
grp: Teams prepare a pitch for 3 minutes.
3–4 students act as investors with an imaginary €100,000 to share.
Investors announce who gets their money and why.

end: Who got the most investment? Would you really buy it?

name: Rank It
desc: Put five things in order. Then agree on one ranking with your partner.
instr: Put these in order from best (1) to worst (5). Then compare with a partner and agree on one ranking.

ind: The student ranks the five and explains each position.
You give your ranking and disagree on at least two.
Agree on one ranking together.
pair: Each student ranks alone (30 seconds).
Pairs compare and must agree on one ranking in two minutes.
Pairs join another pair and agree again.
grp: Show the slide. Students rank individually.
Ask a few students for their number one and last. Count hands for each option.
Build a class ranking on the board.

end: Which ranking caused the biggest argument?

name: Questions Only
desc: Improvise a scene where you can only speak in questions.
instr: Act out the scene with your partner, but you can ONLY speak in questions. Hesitate, repeat or answer with a statement… and you're out!
ex: A: Excuse me, is this your dog? B: Why are you asking? A: Didn't you see it ate my sandwich? B: Are you sure it was my dog?
cards: Ordering in a very strange restaurant
A job interview for a superhero
Returning a broken phone to the shop
Two strangers stuck in a lift
A parent and a teenager at 3 am

ind: You and the student act the scene, questions only.
The first one to make a statement loses the round.
Do three quick rounds, then review question forms that came up.
pair: Pairs act the scene for one minute.
When someone makes a statement or hesitates, swap in a new partner (or restart).
Count how many questions each pair managed.
grp: Two volunteers act at the front.
When one makes a mistake, the class shouts 'Out!' and a new student replaces them.
Keep the same scene running as long as possible.

end: What was the funniest question of the day?

name: Slide Roulette
desc: PowerPoint karaoke: give an expert talk on a ridiculous topic you've never seen before.
instr: You are a world expert on this topic. Give a two-minute talk using the three points. You've never seen the slide before… improvise!
ph: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about…

cards.t: The secret life of office chairs
Why cats are better managers than humans
Pizza as a form of art
Teaching your grandmother to use TikTok
The economics of a children's lemonade stand
Why we should all have a nap at work
The dangers of being too polite
A day in the life of a supermarket trolley

ind: The student sees the slide for the first time and talks for two minutes.
You ask two 'audience' questions at the end.
Swap roles on the next slide.
pair: Pairs take turns presenting to each other.
The listener asks one question at the end.
Give feedback on linkers used.
grp: Choose a volunteer (or use Pick a student). They see the slide for the first time with the class.
Start the timer: two minutes.
The audience asks two questions. Applause is mandatory!

end: Who was the most convincing expert today?

name: What Happens If…?
desc: Say what always happens in everyday situations, then compare with the answer.
instr: What always happens? Answer with a full sentence. Then add one more 'If…' fact about your own life.
ex: If you don't sleep, you feel tired. If I drink coffee after 6 pm, I can't sleep.

cards.t: If you don't water a plant…
If you mix red and blue…
If you leave milk out of the fridge…
If you don't charge your phone…
If you eat too much chocolate…
If you press the snooze button…
If you drop your phone in water…
If you don't wear sun cream at the beach…
If you shout in a library…
If you don't practise a language…

ind: Show the beginning. The student finishes it before you reveal the answer.
Ask: 'And in your case?' The student makes one personal zero-conditional sentence.
Correct the structure: present + present (no 'will').
pair: Partners take turns finishing the sentence before the reveal.
After each card, each partner says one personal 'If I…, I…' habit.
Find one habit you both share.
grp: Show the card. Students write their ending on a mini whiteboard or say it to a partner.
Reveal: who said the same?
Pick two students to share a personal 'If I…' habit.

end: Write three 'If…' facts about your daily routine.

name: Chain Reaction
desc: Build a chain of consequences: each result becomes the next 'If…'.
instr: Continue the chain. Take the result of the last sentence and start a new one with 'If…'. How long can you keep it going?
ex: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home. If I stay at home, I'll watch films all day. If I watch films all day, I'll eat too much popcorn…
cards: If I win the match on Saturday,…
If I wake up late tomorrow,…
If I go to the party tonight,…
If I pass all my exams,…
If my best friend visits me,…
If I save some money this month,…
If the teacher gives us homework,…
If I miss the last bus tonight,…

ind: You and the student take turns adding one link to the chain.
Each link must start with the result of the previous one.
Stop at 8 links and read the whole chain back.
pair: Partners alternate links for one minute (use the timer).
Count the links. Can they beat their score on the next card?
Swap who starts.
grp: Students stand in a circle. Each adds one link.
Anyone who hesitates for more than 5 seconds or makes a mistake sits down.
Last students standing win.

end: What was the funniest chain? Where did it end?

name: What Would You Do?
desc: Real-life dilemmas: what would you do, and why?
instr: Read the situation. What would you do? Explain why, and say what you definitely wouldn't do.
ph: If I were in that situation, I'd…
If it were me, I might…
q: Would your answer change if nobody was watching?
cards: You see your friend's partner on a date with someone else.
A shop gives you too much change.
You win a free trip, but it's on your best friend's wedding day.
Your boss offers you a promotion in another city.
You break a glass at a friend's house and nobody sees it.
A stranger asks you to look after their dog for an hour.
You hear your neighbours arguing loudly at 2 am.
Someone in a restaurant is talking very loudly on the phone.
You get a message meant for someone else.
You're offered your dream job, but the salary is lower.
Your friend asks what you think of their terrible haircut.

ind: The student answers and explains. Push with 'And if…?' to change one detail.
Share what you would do and disagree on purpose.
Note errors with 'would' + infinitive and 'If I were…'.
pair: Each partner answers; the other asks 'What if…?' with a new detail.
They must find one thing they would both do.
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the dilemma and give 30 seconds to think.
Vote with hands for the two most popular options.
Ask one student from each side to justify their choice.

end: Which dilemma was the hardest? Did anyone change their mind?

name: Imagine If…
desc: Imagine a different world and describe how life would change.
instr: Imagine this was true. How would life be different? Think about school, work, free time and your own day.
cards: If we only needed to sleep one hour a day
If everybody spoke the same language
If it was summer all year
If cars were banned in cities

ind: The student gives at least three consequences.
Ask about their personal day: 'What would you do?'
Correct 'would' in the result clause and past simple in the if-clause.
pair: Partners take turns adding one consequence each, for one minute.
Then decide: would the world be better or worse?
Share the best idea with the class.
grp: Show the card. Groups list as many consequences as possible in 2 minutes.
Groups read their lists. Repeated ideas don't count.
The group with the most original ideas wins.

end: Which world would you like to live in?

name: Sliding Doors
desc: One small change in the past. How would everything have been different?
instr: Imagine this had happened differently. Build a chain: what would or wouldn't have happened?
ex: If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met Ana. If I hadn't met Ana, I wouldn't have joined the choir…
cards: You missed the bus this morning.
The Titanic had seen the iceberg in time.
You had been born in another country.
The internet had never been invented.
You had chosen a different school or job.
You hadn't gone out last Saturday.
You had said yes to the last invitation you said no to.
Your favourite band had never formed.
You hadn't met your best friend.

ind: The student builds a chain of at least four third-conditional links.
Ask about real regrets: 'Is there anything you would have done differently?'
Drill the contraction: 'I'd have' / 'I wouldn't have'.
pair: Partners alternate links until they reach something surprising.
Then each shares one real past decision and how life could have been different.
Report the funniest chain to the class.
grp: Show the card. One student starts, the next continues the chain.
Write the chain on the board as it grows.
At the end, the class reads it aloud together.

end: Is there a small decision in your life that changed everything?

name: Mixed Up Lives
desc: A different past, a different present: talk about who you'd be now.
instr: Imagine this had been different in the past. How would your life be different NOW?
ph: If I had…, I would be… now.
If I hadn't…, I wouldn't have… now.
If I were…, I would have… (past)
ex: If I had studied medicine, I would be working in a hospital now. If I weren't so shy, I would have spoken to her yesterday.
cards: If you had been born 100 years ago…
If you had studied something completely different…
If you had grown up in another country…
If you had never learnt to use a computer…
If you had been born a twin…
If you had become famous as a child…
If you weren't afraid of anything… (what would you have done last year?)
If you were a morning person… (what would you have done this morning?)
If you had moved house five years ago…
If you had saved all the money you've spent on coffee…
If you spoke five languages… (what would you have done differently?)
If you had said yes to your first job offer…

ind: The student answers with at least two mixed-conditional sentences.
Ask them to switch: past→present, then present→past.
Highlight the two patterns on the board.
pair: Partners take turns. The listener checks the tenses and asks one follow-up.
After each card, partners compare: whose 'other life' sounds better?
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the card and give a minute of thinking time.
Pick students to share; the class identifies which pattern they used.
Finish with a quick correction round.

end: Write one mixed conditional about your own life.
